title: A Glimpse of American Medicine
paragraphs: I studied abroad at Johns Hopkins University Hospital in the United States for 12 weeks, from March 26 to June 15. I rotated through three departments, emergency medicine, pediatric neurology and medical oncology, and took part in the medical team in the same position as the local students. The three months were very short and passed in the blink of an eye, but I believe that those three months, in which I studied English and medicine hard every day and tried to keep up with medical students who are among the best in the world, will hold great meaning in my life from now on. I would like to describe below what I learned in these three months.

It may be obvious, but the "standard medicine of Japan" that I had been learning through clinical clerkships in Japan was often not normal in the United States. The foremost example is the shortness of hospital stays. In medical oncology in particular, discharge schedules were set not by the day but by the hour, and I could sense the determination not to let anyone stay in hospital needlessly. It apparently takes into account not only the patient but also medical costs, the burden on the family and the capacity of the hospital. For example, in Japan there are cases in which patients without particular symptoms are hospitalized for a long time for chemotherapy of blood cancer, but such cases are very rare here. What can be done in the outpatient clinic is done there more and more, and even when fever and the like are expected, patients are actively discharged after being carefully taught how to deal with such situations.

Another thing that surprised me was the thorough respect for the patient's will. In Japan, too, the importance of informed consent has come to be advocated, but I felt that it is still insufficient. In emergency medicine in particular, a system was in place in which "how far they want us to go" is decided by the patient's will. For example, even for a test that the doctor thinks should be done to find the cause, if the patient refuses, the patient is readily discharged. There are many people who have come to the hospital to have their suffering removed, not to undergo tests that would cause them more suffering.

As I saw such cases, I could not help feeling that Japan may be somewhat prone to excessive medical care, for better and for worse. In the United States, especially in medical oncology, I often saw scenes in which, when the prognosis was expected to be poor, the doctor explained it to the patient with a kind of attitude of "resignation," and I did not feel at all that this was wrong. I felt the need for the whole country to think about what kind of medical care should be provided, always keeping the patient in mind.

I realized that American medicine is very highly specialized, for better and for worse. For example, I was able to do a clerkship in medical oncology, which is not common in Japan. Medical oncology is an internal medicine department that specializes in cancer, and anyone with cancer is hospitalized in it. For that reason, research on chemotherapy regimens may advance by leaps and bounds, but on the other hand, because medical oncology handles such a wide range of cancers, consults to each specialty department end up being necessary, and I sometimes felt it was inefficient.

There was also an internal medicine department specializing in infectious diseases that gives appropriate consults on the use of antibiotics. Certainly, in these days when the emergence of resistant bacteria through the abuse of antibiotics is a problem, such specialists may be useful, but if each internist had thorough knowledge of antibiotics and infectious diseases, it seemed not to be an absolutely necessary department.

Thus, there is a debate about whether the unique specialty internal medicine departments created by the United States are absolutely necessary, but at least by knowing of their existence, I think I was able to view objectively the systems that may be weaknesses of Japanese medicine.

I also thought that the distribution of tasks to other healthcare professionals is very advanced in the United States. There were technicians who specialized in drawing blood cultures and specialist nurses who efficiently looked for discharge destinations and managed things so that discharge went smoothly, and the division of labor had advanced to the point of seeming luxurious. Even among nurses, those with specialist qualifications could write prescriptions and place orders, and I thought it was a very rational system for resolving the shortage of doctors.

I had heard before going to the United States that American medical education is excellent, so I was greatly looking forward to experiencing it. Johns Hopkins University, as one would expect of a university hospital at the top level in the United States, had a great many lectures and conferences. In particular, since there were lectures using free time such as before work started in the morning and during lunch breaks, no time was wasted and it was very efficient.

Education was also properly carried out by making good use of students as members of the team. Students go to the hospital every morning earlier than the residents and examine the patients. After that, they receive feedback on it, look up the literature on their own and present, helping the team to realize evidence-based medicine. I do not know how much the senior physicians rely on the information students bring, but I thought that American doctors are all good at praising and skillfully raise students' motivation.

This is what I was able to learn. Through a great deal of effort and "keenness," the three months were very fulfilling. I was able to understand the points to learn from the American system and the wonderful points of Japanese medicine, and I think this will surely be an experience that serves me in the future. Finally, I express my heartfelt gratitude to the doctors of the Nagoya University School of Medicine, beginning with Dr. 伊藤勝基, Dr. 坂本純一, Dr. 粕谷英樹, Dr. 尾崎紀夫, Dr. 祖父江元 and Dr. 室原豊明, who supported this study abroad, to the seniors who helped me in the preparatory course, and to everyone at the International Exchange Office.
